name: Yakkha
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: The rules for stress assignment can be laid out as follows: by default, the first syllable carries main stress. Closed syllables, however, attract stress. If there are closed syllables, the main stress moves to the last closed syllable, as long as it is not the final syllable of a word [...] (but only up to the penultimate syllable). [...] Examples like ˈkam.ni.bak 'friend' show that the stress never moves to the final syllable, even when the syllable is heavy. Patterns where the final syllable is stressed are possible though, because prefixes are not part of the stress domain. In monosyllabic nouns that host a possessive prefix, the stress generally remains on the stem
new_statements.citation: Schackow, Diana. 2015. A grammar of Yakkha (Studies in Diversity Linguistics 7). Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.17169/langsci.b66.106.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 3 Phonology, section 3.4 'Stress assignment', p. 57 (rule) and p. 59 (no final stress; prefixes outside domain); secondary stress p. 61
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress is initial by default; if the word contains closed (heavy) syllables, main stress falls on the rightmost closed syllable that is not word-final (i.e. stress may move rightward only as far as the penult); word-final syllables are never stressed within the stem+suffix domain. Prefixes (possessive a-, u-, reduplicative prefixes) are outside the stress domain, so prefixed monosyllabic stems surface with final stress (a.ˈpaŋ 'my house').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Author states it is hard to tell whether there is secondary stress; none detected even in five-syllable words. Secondary stress is clearly audible in compounds, on the first syllable of the second member (main stress stays on the first syllable of the whole compound, and such compounds may override the ban on final stress, e.g. ˈko.len.ˌluŋ). In inflected verb forms secondary stress can appear on the verb stem (ˌndum.men.cu.ˈŋan.na).
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Lexicalized monosyllabic kin terms with possessive prefix take initial stress on the prefix (ˈa.mum 'grandmother') but revert when the prefix changes (u.ˈmum); (ii) nominalizing clitics =na/=ha, unlike other clitics, count as part of the verb's stress domain; (iii) triplicated ideophonic adverbs have lengthened, stressed final syllable ([se.re.ˈreː] 'drizzling'); (iv) in noun-verb complex predicates and co-compounds each component carries its own stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word = stem plus suffixes; prefixes and phrase-level clitics (case, discourse markers) are excluded and do not affect stress. Description based on the Tumok village dialect; impressionistic (no instrumental study).
new_statements.identity_note: Schackow (2015) describes the Tumok (Nepali: Tamaphok) village dialect of Yakkha, Sankhuwa Sabha district, eastern Nepal; the author notes at least four Yakkha dialects. Glottocode yakk1236 (ISO ybh) is the language-level code; no separate dialect glottocode identified.

sources.note: Ch. 3 Phonology, section 3.4 'Stress assignment' (pp. 57-61): default main stress on the first syllable; closed syllables attract stress, so main stress moves to the last closed syllable provided it is not word-final; prefixes and phrasal clitics are outside the stress domain (except nominalizers =na/=ha on verbs); secondary stress only clearly audible in compounds (first syllable of second member) and on verb stems in long inflected forms; triplicated ideophonic adverbs exceptionally have final stress with vowel lengthening.
